metric.dependency_simplicity.normalization_rule: 0-100 scale, 100 = no external toolchain/runtime/package-manager dependency required for a standard idiomatic build; scored by counting distinct external tools/runtimes needed for a representative build+run cycle.
raw_observations: Zig ships a single self-contained toolchain (zig binary) bundling compiler, linker, bundled libc (musl/mingw/wasi-libc), and package manager (build.zig.zon) - no separate build system or package manager binary required.
Standard library is dependency-free for most programs; no system libc required by default on many targets.
build.zig is Zig code executed by the same compiler, eliminating a second build-DSL dependency (unlike CMake+Make or npm+webpack stacks).
Cross-compilation and dependency fetching are integrated in-tree via the same zig executable.
FFI-linked native libraries still reintroduce systems-level dependency management similar to C/C++, which is reflected as a minor deduction.
metric.dependency_simplicity.score_basis: Single compiler binary provides compiler+linker+build system+package manager+cross-compilation; no external runtime needed for standard builds. Score 92 reflects near-minimal dependency footprint with minor deduction for FFI scenarios.

metric.portability_design_platform_neutr.normalization_rule: 0-100 scale, 100 = language design imposes no platform-specific runtime assumption and provides first-class compile-time target abstraction/cross-compilation without extra tooling.
raw_observations: Zig's language design centers on cross-compilation as a first-class built-in feature: any zig install can target any supported triple without a separate cross toolchain.
std.builtin.Target and comptime target queries allow clean compile-time OS/arch branching without preprocessor macros.
Zig bundles libc implementations (musl, mingw-w64, wasi-libc) enabling static, portable binaries across Linux/Windows/macOS/WASI/freestanding from one host.

No mandatory GC runtime or OS-specific runtime service is baked into the language, allowing freestanding/embedded/WASI targeting directly - stronger neutrality than JVM-bound languages or Go's baked-in scheduler.
Explicit allocator passing avoids implicit OS-specific heap/thread assumptions, reinforcing platform-neutral core design.
Ecosystem breadth of currently supported/tested platforms is excluded here per methodology; this evaluates only architectural/design neutrality.
metric.portability_design_platform_neutr.score_basis: Explicit-allocator, no-hidden-runtime, built-in cross-compilation, and comptime target-conditional design yield a high score of 90; minor deduction because some std library paths still assume POSIX-like semantics.
